Constitutional Protection of Privacy in India

Privacy is connected with human dignity, personal liberty and the ability of individuals to exercise control over aspects of their lives, including personal information.

Article 21 of the Constitution of India protects life and personal liberty. It provides that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

The Supreme Court has interpreted the constitutional protection of life and liberty to include several rights necessary for human dignity and personal freedom.

The Right to Privacy Judgment of 2017

On 24 August 2017, a 9-judge Bench of the Supreme Court unanimously recognised the right to privacy as a constitutionally protected fundamental right in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India.

The Court held that privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty protected under Article 21 and is also connected with the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.

The judgment recognises privacy as part of human dignity, liberty and individual autonomy. Its significance extends beyond physical privacy to matters involving personal choices and information.

Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, 2017: A unanimous 9-judge Supreme Court Bench recognised privacy as a fundamental right protected under Article 21 and other relevant guarantees in Part III.

The right to privacy is not absolute. State interference with this right must satisfy applicable constitutional requirements, including legality, a legitimate aim and proportionality. The existence of the right does not prohibit every lawful use of personal information.

Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, numbered Act 22 of 2023, following presidential assent on 11 August 2023.

The Act establishes a framework for the processing of digital personal data while recognising both individuals' interests in protecting their personal information and the need to process such information for lawful purposes.

Important Terms

TermMeaning
Data PrincipalThe individual to whom personal data relates; for a child under 18, this includes the parents or lawful guardian, and for a person with disability, the lawful guardian acting on the person's behalf.
Data FiduciaryA person or entity that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data, alone or with others.
Consent ManagerAn entity registered with the Data Protection Board that enables Data Principals to give, manage, review and withdraw consent through an accessible platform.

For example, when a service provider determines why and how a customer's personal information will be processed, the provider may act as a Data Fiduciary. The identifiable customer is the Data Principal.

Status of the Act and Rules: 16 November 2026

The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were published through Gazette notification G.S.R. 846(E), dated 13 November 2025. The Government also issued commencement notification G.S.R. 843(E) for different provisions of the 2023 Act.

The Act and Rules have a phased implementation schedule. The notification of the Rules does not mean that every substantive obligation and individual right became enforceable immediately.

As of the content cutoff of 16 November 2026, the framework for registration of Consent Managers had taken effect on 13 November 2026. Other significant provisions concerning the rights of Data Principals, obligations of Data Fiduciaries and the Board's inquiry and penalty processes were scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027.

The Data Protection Board of India is the statutory body established under the Act for functions assigned to it. The commencement and exercise of particular functions depend on the applicable notified provisions.

Enactment, notification and commencement

A law may be enacted before all its provisions become operative. A set of rules may also be notified before every rule commences. For the DPDP framework, the legally relevant status must therefore be determined from the notified commencement dates, not merely from the year appearing in the Act or Rules.

How Security Mechanisms Relate to Privacy

Protecting personal information requires different safeguards for different purposes. The correct safeguard depends on whether the problem involves unauthorised reading, alteration, identity verification, inappropriate access or unnecessary collection.

Protecting Confidentiality

Encryption reduces the risk that an unauthorised person can read protected information. Access controls and appropriate sharing permissions further restrict who may obtain it.

Protecting Integrity

Digital signatures and suitable integrity-verification mechanisms can help detect unauthorised alteration. Encryption alone does not necessarily provide this assurance.

Verifying Identity and Origin

Authentication checks a claimed identity. A digital signature can verify that a signing operation corresponds to a particular private key, while trustworthy certificates help associate the corresponding public key with the claimed signer.

Protecting Privacy Through Responsible Processing

Data minimisation limits unnecessary personal-data collection and use. Purpose-based handling, appropriate retention, restricted disclosure and technical security measures work together to reduce privacy risks.

Applying the Distinctions

Consider an online government application containing a citizen's identity details. If an unauthorised person reads the application, confidentiality has been compromised. If the application is altered without permission, integrity has been compromised. If authorised officials cannot retrieve it, availability has been affected.

If an officer must prove identity before accessing the application, authentication is relevant. If the officer may view but not modify the record, authorisation is relevant. If the applicant must verify that the issued electronic certificate is genuine and unchanged, a digital signature may be relevant.

Finally, if the application collects unrelated personal information, the concern is data minimisation and privacy, even if the collected information is strongly encrypted.

Prelims focus

  • Article 21 protects life and personal liberty.
  • Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India: 24 August 2017; unanimous 9-judge Bench; privacy recognised as a fundamental right.
  • Digital Personal Data Protection Act: 2023; Act 22 of 2023; presidential assent on 11 August 2023.
  • Digital Personal Data Protection Rules: 2025; phased commencement.
  • Consent Manager registration framework: effective from 13 November 2026.
  • Major remaining DPDP provisions: scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027.
  • Trap: Enactment or notification does not necessarily mean that every provision has commenced.

Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, Writ Petition (Civil) 494 of 2012, judgment dated 24 August 2017; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sections 1-2 and 18; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Gazette notifications G.S.R. 843(E) and G.S.R. 846(E), 13 November 2025, commencement provisions; Press Information Bureau, Consent Manager Registration Framework Comes into Effect, 14 November 2026, status and commencement dates. Current-status cutoff: 16 November 2026.]
